newsitem.title: BULGARIA: EU to discuss Bulgaria funding before IMF deal.
newsitem.headline: EU to discuss Bulgaria funding before IMF deal.

text.p: The European Union (EU) mission is expected to visit Bulgaria March 17-18 and is prepared to discuss financial help even before a funding deal with the International Monetary Fund is in place, an EU official said on Tuesday.

"At present we are ready to mobilise a negotiation team even in advance of a final agreement with the International Monetary Fund," head of EU representation office in Sofia Thomas O'Sullivan told a news conference.
The team, to be led by EU external relations commissioner Hans van den Broek, is expected to start talks with the caretaker government on a "substantial loan", said O'Sullivan.
"The final figure will depend on negotiations with the IMF and the G-24 group of donor countries," said O'Sullivan.

The interim cabinet said last week it will prepare a preliminary agreement with the IMF by the end of this week, that will include the implementation of a currency board mechanism aimed to stabilise the crumbling financial system.

The European Union has granted 20 million ecus ($23 million) to support 500,000 low income households, which is 20 percent of all Bulgarian households, and 63,000 residents of some 570 social institutions, said O'Sullivan.
The payments, due to begin at end of March, are expected to be handed out through municipal welfare offices for the next four months.

The Balkan country is suffering an unprecedented crisis precipitated by delays in reforms over the past seven years. Mismanagement by the previous Socialist administration and asset stripping of banks and factories have left the economy in disarray.

Bulgaria's President Petar Stoyanov in January drew the world spotlight onto his country's economic crisis when he raised the prospect of Bulgaria defaulting on its external debt unless it received urgent help.
Bulgaria owes $1 billion in foreign debt payments this year alone and relies on external support and privatisation proceeds as source of cash.
The interim cabinet asked the Paris Club of official creditors last week to roll over for next year $50 million payments due this year.
